prompt: With three home replicas, which required write/read counts force every read group to overlap every completed write group, while allowing one replica to be unavailable for both operations?

options.text: One write acknowledgement, one read response
options.explanation: Wrong. 1 + 1 = 2, which isn't greater than 3, so a read can hit a replica the write never reached and return stale data.

options.text: Three write acknowledgements, one read response
options.explanation: Overlap holds (3 + 1 = 4 > 3), but any single replica failure blocks *all writes*, because W needs all three. It fails the 'tolerate one down' requirement.

options.text: Two write acknowledgements, two read responses
options.explanation: Correct. 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, so quorums overlap in at least one replica. And since each needs only 2 of 3, one replica can be down and both reads and writes still succeed.

options.text: One write acknowledgement, three read responses
options.explanation: Overlap holds (1 + 3 = 4 > 3), but any single replica failure blocks *all reads*, and every read waits for the slowest replica.

workedExample: With three home replicas, any two-replica read group overlaps any two-replica write group. Both can still form when one replica is unavailable. Requiring all three would block that operation during the failure; requiring only one each permits disjoint groups. This counting argument establishes intersection, not linearizability.

link.title: Dynamo: Amazon's highly available key-value store (SOSP 2007)

prompt: Your 6-node ring gives each node a single token. Node C fails permanently. What problem do virtual nodes (many tokens per physical node) solve here?

options.text: Vnodes can spread failed-node ranges and recovery work across more peers instead of concentrating primary-range ownership on one successor.
options.explanation: Correct. Vnodes turn 'one neighbour takes everything' into 'everyone takes a little'. That balances steady-state load and parallelises recovery.

options.text: Vnodes let the ring keep serving C's keys without any replicas
options.explanation: Wrong. Vnodes are about *placement*, not redundancy. Availability for C's keys still comes from the other N - 1 replicas.

options.text: Vnodes eliminate the need for consistent hashing
options.explanation: Wrong. Vnodes *are* a refinement of consistent hashing: more points per node on the same ring.
Wrong. Token placement has nothing to do with transactional guarantees across keys.

workedExample: A single-token primary range can pass to one successor. Several virtual ranges can distribute ownership and streaming work across multiple surviving peers. Token successors can still share a physical machine, so many tokens do not imply equally many independent destinations. Replication and measured placement remain necessary; vnodes do not create redundancy by themselves.
